html:
A cloth shop opened in Edo in 1673 by the merchant Mitsui Takatoshi. It grew into the Mitsukoshi department store and was the root of the Mitsui business group.

At the time, kimono cloth was sold mostly to rich clients at their homes, on credit settled once or twice a year, with prices haggled each time. Echigoya broke with this. Its slogan promised cash sales at fixed, marked prices, and it would cut cloth to any length. This let ordinary townspeople of growing Edo buy, and the shop's turnover soared. Rival merchants fought it, but it prospered and opened branches in Kyoto and Osaka.

The Mitsui also became money changers, handling funds for the Tokugawa shogunate. After the Meiji Restoration they backed the new government and built one of the great zaibatsu, family business empires that included a bank, a trading company and mines. Mitsui firms remain among Japan's largest companies.
